title: New Every Morning
subtitle: Lamentations in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Lamentations is a book of tears for a fallen city. Jerusalem sits alone like a widow. The roads to Zion are empty, the gates have sunk into the ground, the gold has grown dim, and a fox walks across the holy mountain. And at the very center of the book, in the dark, a poet remembers something, and says it out loud: his mercies are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

This book walks through it in thirty short poems, in five parts, one for each chapter of the old lament. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with what the city left behind—a lamp burning low, an ember in the ash, a lyre lying in the dust—and leave the faces to your imagination. If you are grieving, you are welcome here, and you don't have to hurry to the hopeful part.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Lamentations alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: How the City Sits
parts.epigraph: How the city sits solitary, that was full of people!
parts.lightName: Light of How the City Sits
parts.lightHint: Near 'how' (Lamentations 1:1) in Part 1: How the City Sits

parts.title: Cry Out in the Night
parts.epigraph: Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches!
parts.lightName: Light of Cry Out in the Night
parts.lightHint: Near 'a cloud' (Lamentations 2:1) in Part 2: Cry Out in the Night

parts.title: New Every Morning
parts.epigraph: It is because of Y ahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail.
parts.lightHint: Near 'walled in' (Lamentations 3:7–9) in Part 3: New Every Morning

parts.title: How the Gold Has Become Dim
parts.epigraph: How the gold has become dim! The most pure gold has changed!
parts.lightName: Light of How the Gold Has Become Dim
parts.lightHint: Near 'stones in the street' (Lamentations 4:1) in Part 4: How the Gold Has Become Dim

paintings.title: how
paintings.epigraph: “How the city sits solitary, that was full of people!”
paintings.poem:
the market stalls are standing.
the doors are standing.
the well still has its rope.

only the people
are gone.

that is how the book begins.
not with a reason,
not with a lesson,
just a long look
down an empty street

and one small word
that is almost a cry:

how.

paintings.title: in the night
paintings.epigraph: “She weeps bitterly in the night. Her tears are on her cheeks.”
paintings.poem:
the day has chores in it.
bread, water, the door, the fire.

it's at night
that grief sits up.

she weeps in the night,
the poem says,
and her tears are on her cheeks,

not wiped away yet,
not explained,
just there
where anyone who came close
could see them.

if that is you tonight,
you are in good company.
you are not the first
to cry in the dark
and be written down
in the Bible.10

paintings.title: the roads mourn
paintings.epigraph: “The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to the solemn assembly.”
paintings.poem:
no feet on them now.
no singing up the hill
at festival time,
no children running ahead.

grass in the wheel ruts.
a lizard on a warm stone.

even the roads,
the poet says,
are mourning.

grief does that.
it gets into everything:
the path you used to walk,
the day of the week
you used to go.

it isn't foolish
to find it there.

paintings.title: is it nothing to you
paintings.epigraph: “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?”
paintings.poem:
the travelers keep walking.
they have their own errands,
their own long roads.

and the city calls after them
from the rubble:
is it nothing to you?

it's the oldest question
anyone in pain has asked.
does anyone see?

this whole book
is a hand on the sleeve
of whoever is passing.

stop a moment.
look.

some sorrow
only asks
to be seen.

paintings.title: open hands
paintings.epigraph: “Zion spreads out her hands. There is no one to comfort her.”
paintings.poem:
again and again
the chapter says it:
no one to comfort her.

so she does
the only thing left.
she spreads out her hands.

not a fist.
not a door slammed shut.
open palms,
empty,
held out into the air,

the way a child
holds up her arms
to be lifted.

an empty hand
is still a prayer.

paintings.title: a cloud
paintings.epigraph: “How has the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger!”
paintings.poem:
the poet doesn't pretend.
he says it plainly:
a cloud came down
over the city
and the light went out of it,
and he names who he thinks
let it come.

the Bible lets him say it.
it doesn't cut the line
or tidy it up.

some grief is angry,
and aimed at heaven,
and heaven
keeps it in the book.

you can bring God
the hard sentence too.
he has heard it before.

paintings.title: gates in the ground
paintings.epigraph: “Her gates have sunk into the ground. He has destroyed and broken her bars.”
paintings.poem:
gates were for keeping safe,
for closing at dusk,
for old men sitting in their shade.

now they lie half buried,
hinges in the dust,
the great bars broken.

nothing keeps anything out.
nothing keeps anything in.

some losses are like that.
the thing that held your life together
is lying in the dirt,

and all you can do
is sit beside it
and say so.

paintings.title: they keep silence
paintings.epigraph: “The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground. They keep silence.”
paintings.poem:
the old men sit down
on the bare ground
and say nothing.

dust on their heads.
rough cloth on their shoulders.

no speeches.
no answers.
they have lived long enough
to know
there aren't any yet.

if you are sitting
with someone in grief,
you may not need words.

sit down.
stay.

the ground is big enough
for two.

paintings.title: as big as the sea
paintings.epigraph: “For your breach is as big as the sea. Who can heal you?”
paintings.poem:
the poet searches
for something to compare it to,
something to say
that might help.

he tries one picture,
then another.

in the end
the only thing big enough
is the sea.

a wound as wide as the sea.
who can heal that?

he doesn't answer.
not yet.

but he kept reaching for words
because he wanted to comfort her.

that reaching
is already a kind of love.

paintings.title: pour out your heart
paintings.epigraph: “Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord.”
paintings.poem:
not a little.
not politely.
not only the parts
that sound like faith.

pour it out
the way you'd empty a jar,
upside down,
every last drop,
the grit at the bottom too.

get up in the night
and do it.

water poured on the ground
can't be gathered up again,

but it isn't lost.
it goes before the face
of the Lord.

paintings.title: walled in
paintings.epigraph: “He has walled me about, so that I can’t go out.”
paintings.poem:
cut stone on every side.
paths that bend back
to where they started.

he calls out,
and it feels like the prayer
hits the ceiling.

this is the darkest room
in the whole book,
and it sits right in the middle.

it goes this low
before it turns.

if you are in the room
where the walls are close
and the prayers come back unopened,

keep reading.
the same voice
is about to say
something else.

paintings.title: I forgot
paintings.epigraph: “Y ou have removed my soul far away from peace. I forgot prosperity.”
paintings.poem:
not just that things were bad.
he forgot
what good felt like.

the taste of an easy morning.
a table with enough.
a night of plain sleep.

that is the deepest part of grief,
when even the memory
of peace
goes quiet.

my strength has perished,
he says,
and my hope with it.

he writes that down honestly.

and then
he keeps writing.

paintings.title: this I recall
paintings.epigraph: “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.”
paintings.poem:
nothing outside has changed.
the walls are still down.
the streets are still empty.

what changes
is what he chooses
to bring to mind.

he reaches into the ash
of everything he's lost
and finds
one coal still warm.

this I recall.

hope doesn't wait
for the ruins to be rebuilt.
sometimes it begins
with remembering on purpose.

paintings.title: new every morning
paintings.epigraph: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.”
paintings.poem:
yesterday's mercy
was enough for yesterday.

you don't have to ration it
through the dark.

every morning
the light comes up over the rubble,
and with it, kindness
enough for today,
fresh as the dew on the stones.

someone who had lost nearly everything
watched that sun come up
and said to God:
great is your faithfulness.

paintings.title: my portion
paintings.epigraph: ““Yahweh is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.””
paintings.poem:
long ago, when the land was shared out,
every family got a portion:
a field, a vineyard,
a place to belong.

now the fields
belong to strangers.

and the poet looks around
at everything he no longer has,
and says:

the Lord
is my portion.

no one can carry that off.
no army
can march onto that field.

paintings.title: wait quietly
paintings.epigraph: “It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.”
paintings.poem:
not pacing.
not fixing.
not running to the gate
every hour
to see who is coming.

just sitting
in the doorway,
facing east,
hoping.

it is good, he says,
to wait quietly.

quiet isn't giving up.
it's the stillness
of someone who believes
help is on the way.

paintings.title: not forever
paintings.epigraph: “For the Lord will not cast off forever.”
paintings.poem:
the grief is real.
the night is long.

but he does not
hurt us gladly,
and he will not
turn away forever.

paintings.title: heart and hands
paintings.epigraph: “Let’s lift up our heart with our hands to God in the heavens.”
paintings.poem:
first, a searching.
let us look at our ways,
the poet says,
honestly,
and turn around.

then, a lifting.

not just the hands.
anyone can raise their hands.

the heart with them.

whatever is heavy in it,
whatever we have done,
whatever was done to us,

lifted up together,
the way you'd hold up
something broken
to someone
who knows how to mend it.

paintings.title: until
paintings.epigraph: “until Yahweh looks down, and sees from heaven.”
paintings.poem:
his eyes won't stop.
no break, he says.
no pause.

and he isn't ashamed of it.
he tells us
how long he plans to cry:

until the Lord
looks down
and sees.

not until he's over it.
not until it makes sense.

until he is seen.

tears are not a failure of faith.
sometimes they are
how faith keeps watch.

paintings.title: don't be afraid
paintings.epigraph: “Y ou came near in the day that I called on you. Y ou said, “Don’t be afraid.””
paintings.poem:
the lowest place.
water over his head.
a stone across the top.

I am cut off, he said.

and from down there,
where no one could see him,
he called on the Name.

here is what he remembers:
you came near.

not the rescue yet.
first,
a nearness.

and a voice in the dark
saying the thing
every frightened child
needs to hear:

don't be afraid.

paintings.title: stones in the street
paintings.epigraph: “The stones of the sanctuary are poured out at the head of every street.”
paintings.poem:
stones cut
for the house of God
now lie at street corners
where the carts go by.

it is hard to see
what you thought was forever
lying in the dust,

and harder
to walk past it
every day.

grief is like that.
it isn't one moment.
it's the corner
you have to pass
again tomorrow.

paintings.title: clay jars
paintings.epigraph: “how they are esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!”
paintings.poem:
worth their weight in gold,
the poem says,

and now
treated like cheap clay jars,
the kind you use
and break
and toss on the heap.

that is what loss can do.
it tells you
you are common,
used up,
worth nothing.

but read the line again:
the work of the hands
of the potter.

even a clay jar
was made by someone
who shaped it
with care.

paintings.title: no one breaks it
paintings.epigraph: “The young children ask bread, and no one breaks it for them.”
paintings.poem:
of all the sorrows in this book,
this may be the smallest sentence
and the heaviest.

the children ask for bread,
and no one breaks it for them.

the poet doesn't look away,
and neither should we.

somewhere
a child is still asking.

bread is a small thing
to break.

paintings.title: the watchtower
paintings.epigraph: “In our watching we have watched for a nation that could not save.”
paintings.poem:
every morning
up on the wall,
eyes on the far road,
watching for the help
they were counting on.

they watched
until their eyes failed.
the dust on the horizon
was only wind.

most of us have a tower like that:
a person,
a plan,
a rescue we keep watching for
that was never able to save.

it isn't wrong to hope.
it just matters
which way you are facing.

paintings.title: accomplished
paintings.epigraph: “The punishment of your iniquity is accomplished, daughter of Zion. He will no more carry you away into captivity.”
paintings.poem:
after all the dark
of this chapter,
one line of light
near the end:

accomplished.

the hard season
has an end.
no more carrying away.

you may not feel it yet.
the ruins still look like ruins.

but a word
has been spoken over them,

and the weight
you have carried so long
can be set down
in the grass.

paintings.title: remember
paintings.epigraph: “Remember, Y ahweh, what has come on us. Look, and see our reproach.”
paintings.poem:
our houses have other people in them now.
our fields
are someone else's harvest.

remember, Lord.

the last chapter
is a prayer
all the way through.

it doesn't begin with praise.
it begins with a list
of what was lost:
the house, the land,
the father at the table.

sometimes that's how prayer starts.
just telling God
what happened,
and asking him
to keep it in mind.

paintings.title: water for money
paintings.epigraph: “We have drunken our water for money. Our wood is sold to us.”
paintings.poem:
water from our own wells.
wood from our own hills.

and now we pay for it.

it's the small things
grief takes
that surprise you:
a cup of water,
a fire lit
without counting sticks.

if even the simple parts
of your day
feel expensive now,

go gently.
it costs more
to live through a loss
than anyone can see.

paintings.title: the lyre
paintings.epigraph: “Our dance is turned into mourning.”
paintings.poem:
no one at the gate
telling the old stories.
no young men
with their music.

the lyre lies in the dust.
the dancing stopped.

the poet doesn't hurry past it.

but there is another song
in Israel's prayer book
where the same words
turn the other way:
you have turned my mourning
into dancing.

the lyre isn't broken.
it's waiting.

paintings.title: the fox
paintings.epigraph: “You, Yahweh, remain forever. Your throne is from generation to generation.”
paintings.poem:
the holy mountain,
where the songs went up,
where the crowds came in at festival,

a fox trots across it now,
nose down,
unbothered,
between the fallen stones.

that's how empty it is.

and in the very next breath
the poet looks up:

but you, Lord,
remain forever.

the mountain can be emptied.
the throne cannot.

paintings.title: renew our days
paintings.epigraph: “Renew our days as of old.”
paintings.poem:
the book ends
without tying it up.
its very last words
are still grief.

but just before them,
a prayer:
turn us back to you,
and we will be turned.
make our days new
like they used to be.

that is where it leaves you,
in the ruins,
praying.

not healed yet.
turned toward home.

and every morning
the mercy that is new
comes up again
over the broken walls.
